**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 34, verses 3–5:**

The Almighty and Majestic said:

﴿Those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come to us." Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you, the Knower of the unseen, from whom not an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth is hidden, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Record."﴾ ﴿That He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds. Those will have forgiveness and a noble provision.﴾ ﴿But those who strove against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them, for them is a painful torment of a grievous kind.﴾

It is narrated that the one who uttered this statement was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who said, "By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, there is no Hour that will come, nor any Resurrection or gathering." So Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet ﷺ to swear by his Lord in response to Abu Sufyan's oath. It was said that this was a refutation, a denial of his claim, and an affirmation of what he had denied. Nafi' permitted pausing (waqf) on "بَلَى" (balā, "yes"). The majority of readers recited ﴿"لَتَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ"﴾ (la-ta'tiyannakum, "it will surely come upon you") with the "ت" (tā') at the beginning. Abu Hatim transmitted a reading "لَيَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ" (la-ya'tiyannakum) with "ي" (yā'), according to the meaning concerning the resurrection (al-ba'th).

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i (in one of the two transmissions from him) read "عالِمِ" ('ālimi, "the Knower") with a kasra, as a substitute (badal, a noun in apposition replacing the preceding noun) for "رَبِّي" (rabbī, "my Lord"). Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "عالِمُ" ('ālimu) with a damma, on the basis of qat' (a shift to a nominative reading, meaning "He is the Knower"). It is also possible that "عالِمُ" is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being "لا يَعْزُبُ" (lā ya'zubu, "is not hidden") and what follows it; the information that the Knower has nothing hidden from Him would then indicate that He has determined its time and knows it. The first aspect is closer to the meaning. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "عَلّامِ" ('allāmi, "the All-Knowing"), an intensive form (mubalagha), in the genitive as a substitute. "يَعْزُبُ" (ya'zubu) means it goes out of sight and becomes distant, and this is how Mujahid and Qatada interpreted it. The majority of readers used a damma on the zāy, while al-Kisa'i and Ibn Wathhab used a kasra; both are two dialectal forms. "مِثْقالُ ذَرَّةٍ" (mithqāla dharra, "an atom's weight") means the measure of its heaviness. This is clear regarding physical bodies, and regarding meanings it is understood by analogy.

Nafi', al-A'mash, and Qatada read "أصْغَرَ" (aṣghara) and "أكْبَرَ" (akbara) with a fatha, in coordination with "ذَرَّةٍ" (dharra). It is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr. In the phrase ﴿إلا في كِتابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ (illā fī kitābin mubīn, "but it is in a clear Record") there is an implied pronoun, whose estimated form is: "إلّا هو في كِتابٍ مُبِينٍ" (illā huwa fī kitābin mubīn, "but He is in a clear Record"). "The clear Record" (al-kitāb al-mubīn) is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfūz).

The lām in ﴿"لِيَجْزِيَ"﴾ (li-yajziya, "that He may reward") may be connected to "لَتَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ" (la-ta'tiyannakum), it may be connected to "لا يَعْزُبُ" (lā ya'zubu), and it may be connected to the sense of the verb within "إلا في كِتابٍ مُبِينٍ" (illā fī kitābin mubīn), since the meaning is: "but I establish it in a clear Record." "Forgiveness" (al-maghfira) is the covering over of sins, and "the noble provision" (al-rizq al-karīm) is Paradise.

His saying "والَّذِينَ" (wa-alladhīna, "and those who") is coordinated (ma'ṭūf) with the first "الَّذِينَ" (alladhīna, "those who"), meaning: "and that He may reward those who strove." "مُعاجِزِينَ" (mu'ājizīna) means seeking to frustrate the power of Allah concerning them. Al-Jahdari, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read "مُعَجِّزِينَ" (mu'ajjizīna) without an alif, meaning they seek to frustrate the power of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, in their own estimation. Ibn al-Zubayr said its meaning is: discouraging from faith whoever wishes it, causing him to become weak in his determination. This is their striving concerning the verses, that is, concerning the matter of the verses. Then the Exalted explained the recompense of those who strive, just as He had previously explained the recompense of the believers.

'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "ألِيمٌ" (alīmun) with a damma as a descriptive adjective (na't) of "الْعَذابُ" (al-'adhāb, "the torment"). The rest read it with a kasra as an adjective of "الرِجْزِ" (al-rijz). "Al-rijz" is the very evil torment. Ibn Muhaysin read "رُجْزٍ" (rujzin) with a damma on the rā'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 34, verses 6–8:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, and it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that when you are completely torn apart, you will be [created] in a new creation?"﴾ ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?" Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far error.﴾

Al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi and others said: "yaran" (see) is coordinated with the verbs before it, though the apparent reading is that it is a new verbal sentence, and that the conjunction "wa" (and) only links one clause to another. It seems the meaning is an informing that those who possess knowledge see the revelation sent down to Muhammad ﷺ as true, and that it guides to the straight path.

His saying: ﴿alladhi unzila﴾ (that which was sent down) is the object of "yaran" (see), "al-haqq" (the truth) is a second object, and "huwa" (it/he) is a pronoun of separation (ʿimad). As for ﴿alladhina utu al-ʿilm﴾ (those who have been given knowledge), it has been said: they are those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam. Qatada said: they are the community of Muhammad ﷺ, the believers in him, whoever they may be. "Yahdi" (guides) means "yurshidu" (directs), and "al-sirat al-mustaqim" (the straight path) is the moderate way, and it intends the path of the Law (sharʿ) and the religion (din).

Then he relates the statement of the disbelievers which they said in a manner of wonder and mockery, i.e., some of them said it to others, just as a man says to someone whom he wishes to amaze: "Shall I show you a joke and a rare curiosity?" Since resurrection was, in their view, among the remote impossibilities, they placed the one who informs of it within the category of those to be wondered at. The governing element of "idha" (when) is a verb implied before it according to what some people said, its estimate being: "He informs you that you will be resurrected when you are torn apart." It is also valid that the governing element be what is in His saying: ﴿innakum lafi khalqin jadid﴾ (indeed you are in a new creation) of the meaning of a verb, since the estimate of the sentence is: "He informs you that indeed you are in a new creation when you are torn apart." Al-Zajjaj said: the governing element of "idha" is ﴿muzziqtum﴾ (you are torn apart), and this is an error and a corruption of the intended meaning; it is not permissible for the governing element to be ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾ (informs you) in any respect. "Muzziqtum" means: by decay and the dispersal of the joints in graves and elsewhere.

The alif of ﴿innakum﴾ is kasra-vowelled because ﴿yunabbi'ukum﴾ carries the meaning of "yaqulu lakum" (says to you), and because of the lam that is in the predicate. "Jadid" means "mujaddid" (renewing).

Their saying: ﴿Aftara﴾ (has he invented) is from the speech of some of them to others. It is the interrogative alif entering upon the alif of connection, so the alif of connection is dropped and the alif remains open, not lengthened. Two days: a day of stations and gatherings, and a day of journeying toward the enemy, is a ta'wib.

And from it is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

We caught up with a tribe who travelled on again after the sun's rays, while we pushed back and the glance inclined.

Mu'arrij said: "awwibi" means "sabbihi" (glorify) in the language of Abyssinia. This is weak and not well known. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the meaning is: lament with him, and the birds assist you in that. He said: when Dawud, peace be upon him, called out with lamentation and yearning, the mountains answered him and the birds gathered above him. He said: from then on the mountains heard an echo.

Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "uwibi" with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the waw, meaning "return with him," that is, in travel or in glorification. He commanded the mountains as one commands a single feminine being, because all that lacks intellect is addressed in this way, and it is referred to and described in this way. From this is the proverb "ya khayla Allah irkabi" (O horses of Allah, mount), and from it: "wa li-hi fiha ma'arib ukhra" (Ta-Ha 20:18). This is common.

Dawud said to that figure in whom the angel had appeared: "What is your opinion of this king, Dawud?" The angel said to him: "An excellent servant, were it not for one flaw in him." And Durayd's saying concerning the Persian, the threaded (one):

The indication in His saying "fi dhalika" (in that) refers to the heaven's encompassing the person and the earth's touching him in every state. "Al-munib" means the one who returns.

Then He mentioned His favour upon Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, as an argument concerning what He bestowed upon Muhammad ﷺ; that is: do not regard this as unlikely, for We have already graciously favoured Our servant long ago with such things. When the illustration for Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was complete, the illustration for them returned to Saba' and what befell them of destruction through disbelief and insolence. The meaning: We said, "O mountains..." And "awwibi" means: return with him, because it is the doubled form of "aba yu'ub" (to return). Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and others said its meaning is: glorify with him, that is, he glorifies and she repeats the glorification with him, that is, she returns the remembrance. Then the verb was doubled for emphasis. It was also said its meaning is: travel with him, because "ta'wib" is the travel of the day: a person would travel by night and then repeat the travel by day, that is, he repeats it, so it is as though he returns it; hence it was called "ta'wib." From this is the poet's saying:

Two days: a day of stations and gatherings, and a day of journeying toward the enemy, is a ta'wib.

And from it is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

We caught up with a tribe who travelled on again after the sun's rays, while we pushed back and the glance inclined.

Mu'arrij said: "awwibi" means "sabbihi" (glorify) in the language of Abyssinia. This is weak and not well known. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the meaning is: lament with him, and the birds assist you in that. He said: when Dawud, peace be upon him, called out with lamentation and yearning, the mountains answered him and the birds gathered above him. He said: from then on the mountains heard an echo.

Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "uwibi" with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the waw, meaning "return with him," that is, in travel or in glorification. He commanded the mountains as one commands a single feminine being, because all that lacks intellect is addressed in this way, and it is referred to and described in this way. From this is the proverb "ya khayla Allah irkabi" (O horses of Allah, mount), and from it: "wa li-hi fiha ma'arib ukhra" (Ta-Ha 20:18). This is common.

Al-A'raj, 'Asim (in one transmission), and a group of the people of Madina read "wa-al-tayra" with a damma, as a conjunction to the wording of His saying "ya jibal" (O mountains). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Ja'far read "wa-al-tayra" with a fatha. It was said: this is a conjunction to "fadlan" (a bounty). This is the view of al-Kisa'i. Sibawayh said: it is on the position of His saying "ya jibal," because the position of an undetermined vocative is in the accusative. Abu 'Amr said: its accusative is by an implied verb whose estimate is: "We subjected the birds."

His saying "wa-alanna lahu al-hadid" (and We made iron pliable for him) means: We made it soft. Qatada and others narrated that iron was for him like wax, requiring no fire in his work. It was said: He gave him a strength by which he could bend iron. It is reported that he met an angel, while Dawud, peace be upon him, took him for a man, and Dawud was disguised, having gone out to ask people about himself in secrecy. Dawud said to that figure in whom the angel had appeared: "What is your opinion of this king, Dawud?" The angel said to him: "An excellent servant, were it not for one flaw in him." Dawud said: "And what is it?" He said: "He takes his provision from the public treasury. If he ate from what his hands made, his virtues would be complete." So Dawud returned and asked Allah to teach him a craft and make it easy for him. Allah taught him the craft of making coats of mail and made iron pliable for him. It was reported that he would make, between his day and his night, a coat of mail worth a thousand dirhams, until he had stored up much of them and his livelihood became ample, and he would spend from the public treasury on the interests of the Muslims.

His saying, exalted is He: "an i'mal sabighat" (that make full coats of mail). It was said that "an" is explanatory (mufassira) and has no place in i'rab. It was also said it is in the accusative position by the removal of the preposition. "Al-sabighat" are the coats of mail that cover, having long rings (quful). Qatada said: Dawud, peace be upon him, was the first to make them. The word "dir' al-hadid" (coat of iron) is feminine, while "dir' al-mar'a" (woman's coat of mail) is masculine.

His saying, exalted is He: "wa-qaddir fi al-sard" (and measure well the links). The commentators differed as to what the measuring concerns in the components of the sard. Sard is the linking of one thing to another of its kind. Al-Shammakh said:

As the leather thongs follow one another in the sard of the bridle.

From it: "sard al-hadith" (the stringing of speech). The coat was called "masrudah" because the rings were joined to rings in it. From it is the poet's saying:

Upon them both are two coats of mail, judged by them, Dawud or the makers of full coats (of mail) are Tubba'.

And Durayd's saying concerning the Persian, the threaded (one):

Ibn Zayd said: the measure commanded is in the size of the ring: do not make them small, lest they become weak and the coat cannot withstand, nor large, lest the wearer be reached through their gaps. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the measure commanded is the nail: he means measure the nails and rings, so that you do not hammer the nail so that it becomes slack (fa-yuslisa; another reading fa-yusalsila), nor thicken it so that it breaks (fa-yanqasim, with the qaf; also narrated with the fa'). Qatada narrated that the coats were before him plates, and so they were heavy; therefore he was commanded to measure in what combines lightness and protection, that is: measure what takes from these two meanings its due share; do not aim at protection so that it becomes heavy, nor at lightness alone so that it removes the defence.

His saying: "wa-i'malu salihan" (and do righteous deeds). Since the command was to Dawud and his family, it is related though no mention of them had preceded, because the meaning indicates them. Then He threatened them with His saying: "Indeed I am Seeing of what you do," that is: its goodness from its evil is not hidden from Me, and according to that will be My recompense for you.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 34, verse 12:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind; its morning [journey] was a month's [travel], and its evening [journey] was a month's [travel]. And We caused a fount of copper to flow for him. And among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord. And whoever deviates from among them from Our command, We will make him taste the punishment of the Blaze.﴾

Al-Hasan said: Solomon, peace be upon him, slaughtered the horses out of grief over what they had caused him to miss of the excellence of the time of the 'Asr prayer, so Allah the Exalted replaced them with something better than them and faster.

The majority recited "al-rīḥa" (الريح) with the accusative, in the sense of: "And for Solomon We subjected the wind." 'Āṣim, in the narration of Abū Bakr, and al-A'raj recited "al-rīḥu" (الريح) with the nominative, on the estimate: "the wind was subjected," or on the basis of the inchoative (al-ibtida'), with the predicate in the prepositional phrase, and that is on the elision of a modifier, its estimate being: "And for Solomon was the subjection of the wind." Al-Hasan recited "wa-li-Sulaymāna al-riyāḥ" (ولسليمان الرياح), and likewise it appears in the plural throughout the whole Qur'an.

(p-165) As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿its morning [journey] was a month's [travel], and its evening [journey] was a month's [travel]﴾, Qatada said: It would cover, in the morning up to near midday, a distance of a month's journey. It is narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: He would set out from Syria from his residence at Tadmur, which the jinn had built for him with stone slabs and columns, and he would take a noon rest at Istakhr, and would set out from there and spend the night in Kabul in the land of Khurasan, or something like this. The whirlwinds would lift his carpet and carry it after that gentle breeze. This carpet, it is related, would carry four thousand horsemen and what resembles them of men and numbers, and would accommodate them. More than this has been related by a great deal, but its lack of soundness, together with its remoteness of resemblance, necessitated its abridgement. The Prophet, may blessings and peace be upon him, has said: ["The best of armies is four thousand"]. And Solomon would not exceed what is good.

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: ["ghadwatuhā shahrun wa-rawḥatuhā shahrun"] (غَدْوَتُها شَهْرٌ ورَوْحَتُها شَهْرٌ). And when Solomon, peace be upon him, wished to reach a people, he would not be perceived until he overshadowed them in the air of the sky.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We caused a fount of copper to flow for him﴾, it is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada that a flowing spring of copper would flow for him in Yemen, from which everything he loved would be made. Al-qitr means copper. A group said: al-qitr is all smelted metal, copper and iron and what runs in their course; springs of it would flow for him. Another group said: rather, the meaning of ﴿"And We caused a fount of copper to flow for him"﴾ is: We melted copper for him, in the manner in which iron became soft for Dawud. They said: Works would be accomplished by him for Solomon while it was cold, without fire. And "'ayn" (عين), on this interpretation, means "melted." They said: copper had not softened nor melted for anyone before him.

As for His saying: ﴿And among the jinn were those who worked﴾, it may be that "man" (مَن) is in the accusative position, as a continuation of what precedes it, with an implied verb whose estimate is: "And We subjected from among the jinn those who work." It may also be that it is in the nominative position, as an inchoative, with the predicate in the prepositional phrase. And "yazigh" (يَزِغْ) means: deviates, i.e., turns aside in disobedience. He said ﴿from Our command﴾ and did not say "from Our will," because nothing occurs in the world that opposes the will, whereas what opposes the command does occur. Ad-Dahhak said: In the codex of 'Abd Allah it is: "And whoever deviates (p-166) from Our command" without "minhum" (مِنهم). As for His saying ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾, it was said: the punishment of the Hereafter. And it was said: rather, an angel had been appointed over them, holding a whip of the fire of the Blaze, so whoever disobeyed, he would strike him and burn him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 34, verse 13:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿They made for him whatever he willed: places of worship, statues, basins like reservoirs, and cooking pots fixed firmly in place. "Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude. And few of My servants are grateful."﴾

Al-maharib (sing. mihrab): the lofty, noble buildings. Qatada said: palaces and mosques. Ibn Zayd said: dwellings. The mihrab is the most noble place in the house, and the mihrab is the place of worship at its most noble. Customary usage became restricted to the place where the imam stands, because of its nobility. From this word is the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

"Like ivory dolls in the mihrabs, or like white [flowers], in the meadow whose blossom shines."

As for al-tamathil (statues): it is said they were made of glass and copper, depicting things that are not living beings. Al-Dahhak said they were depictions of living beings, and that this was permissible in that law.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It was abrogated by the law of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Some people said: depiction is forbidden because images were worshipped. He (the author) reported in al-Hidaya that a sect used to permit depiction and argued with this verse, and that is an error; I do not know of any of the imams of knowledge who permit it.

Al-jawabi is the plural of jabiya, which is the pool into which gathered water flows. The rajaz poet said:

"So I came in the morning to a jabiya, its water flowing, as if it were the skin of the sky going forth."

(p-167) Mujahid said: it is the plural of jawba, which is a great pit in the earth. There is some difficulty with this. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"A bowl of the family of al-Muhallaq negates reproach, like a jabiya of the Iraqi shaykh, overflowing."

Al-Tabari recited it as: "tarukh 'ala Al al-Muhallaq", and it is narrated as "al-sayh" with an unpointed sin, meaning flowing water on the surface of the earth. It is also narrated with shin and kha' dotted, and it is said he meant Kisra. It is also said he meant an unspecified old farmer of the Iraqi countryside, who, because of his weakness, stores water in a jabiya, which is always overflowing; so the bowl was compared to it for its size. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: al-jawabi are the reservoirs.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read kal-jawab without a yā' in pause and in continuation. Abu 'Amr and 'Isa read without a yā' in pause and with a yā' in continuation. Ibn Kathir read with a yā' in both. The reason for omitting the yā' is lightness and brevity, like their omitting it from al-qadi, al-ghazi and al-hadi. Also, since alif-lam replaces tanwin, and the yā' is dropped along with tanwin, it must be dropped with what replaces it, just as they always treat a thing according to the rule of its opposite.

Rasiyat means: firmly fixed because of their size, not things that can be moved or carried, and none can perform their work except the jinn. People explained it as meaning "fixed in place." Then, along with these blessings, they were commanded to act in acts of obedience.

His saying: ﴿"shukran"﴾ may be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: work in acts of obedience while giving thanks from you to Allah for these blessings. It may also be in the accusative as an object, meaning: work a work which is thanks itself, as if prayer, fasting and all worship were themselves the thanks, since they fill its place. In a hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) mounted the pulpit, recited this verse, then said: 'Whoever is given three things has been given the work of thanks: justice in anger and contentment, moderation in poverty and wealth, and fear of Allah in private and in public.'" It is also narrated that Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "O Lord, how can I bear to thank You for Your blessings, when my ability to thank You is itself a blessing from You?" He said: "Now, O Dawud, you have known Me with the true knowledge of Me." Thabit said: it is narrated that the prayer-place of the family of Dawud was never empty of someone standing in prayer by night and by day; they took turns at it continually. It is narrated that Sulayman (peace be upon him) ate barley, fed his family fine bread, and fed the poor refined wheat flour. It is also narrated that he never once was satiated, and when he was asked about this he said: "I fear that I may forget the hungry."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ may be addressed to the family of Dawud, and it may be addressed to the family of Muhammad (ﷺ). In either case it contains warning and encouragement. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) heard a man say: "O Allah, make me one of the few." He said to him: "What is this supplication?" The man said: "I meant His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾." 'Umar said: "Everyone knows better than 'Umar."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And few are they﴾ [Sad: 24], and paucity also in the sense of obscurity is a gift from Allah, blessed and exalted. Therefore this supplication has its excellences.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 34, verse 14:

(p-169) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Then when We decreed death for him, nothing showed them his death except a creature of the earth eating away at his staff. So when he fell down, the jinn saw clearly that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment.﴾

The pronoun refers to Sulayman, peace be upon him. "Qadayna" (We decreed) means: We executed it and brought it into the realm of existence. Otherwise, the final decree concerning him had already preceded in eternity. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, in their accounts, that Sulayman, peace be upon him, used to worship in Bayt al-Maqdis, and every year a tree would sprout in his prayer niche (mihrab). He would ask it about its benefits, its harms, and all its other affairs, and it would inform him. He would order it to be uprooted, and it would be uprooted and its benefits put to use, or it would be planted so that it might propagate. When his death drew near, a tree emerged, and he said to it: "What are you?" It said: "I am the carob tree. I have come out for the ruin of this your kingdom." He said: "Allah would not ruin it while I am alive. But there is no doubt that my appointed time has arrived." So peace be upon him made preparations for it, planted the tree, made from it a staff for himself, and strove diligently in his worship. Then the Angel of Death came to him and informed him that he had been commanded to seize his soul, and that only a short period remained for him. It is related that he then commanded the jinn, and a dome of glass that was transparent was made for him, and he entered into it to worship. He did not make a door for it. He leaned on his staff in a position by which he would remain upright even if he died. Then he passed away, peace be upon him, in that state. It is related that he had provisions for a year prepared within that dome. The jinn used to imagine that he was eating at night, and they did not approach the dome, nor would they enter through the openings that were in its upper parts; whoever of them attempted that would be burned before reaching it. This applies to the period during which Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in the dome. When he died, that awe remained upon the jinn. It is also related that the dome had a door, and that Sulayman commanded some of his household to conceal his death from the jinn and mankind, and to leave him in his state for a year. His purpose in this year was that the jinn should complete a work that had been begun in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him, and it had been decreed that one year's work remained of it, so he wished to see it finished. When a year had passed since his death, he fell from his staff, and the staff had been eaten away by the earth, which is the worm that eats wood. The jinn saw his fall and supposed his death. A bold one among them came and drew near, and was not burned. Then he hesitated and returned, and drew nearer still, until he entered through one of those openings and found Sulayman dead, and informed them of his death. Then that term was examined, and it was determined to be one year. Some people said: the termite was set to eat for a day and a night, then that was measured against its eating in the staff, and it was known that it had been eating for a year. Thus was the indication of the creature of the earth to his death. Among the exegetes, there is much elaboration in these narratives, the foundation of which is what we have mentioned. (p-170) Many of the exegetes said: "a creature of the earth" is the weevil of wood, which is the termite (al-arada). Ibn 'Abbas and al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl read "al-arad" with a fatha on the ra', the plural of aradah, and this supports that interpretation. A group said: "a creature of the earth" is an animal of the earth whose nature is to eat wood, and this exists, and the weevil is not among the creatures of the earth. A group among them, including Abu Hatim the linguist, said: "al-ard" here is a verbal noun from "uridat al-athwab wa al-khashab" when the termite has eaten them, as if he said: the creature of eating which is in that form, by way of wormy infestation.

In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads: "akalat minsa'atahu," and al-minsa'ah is the staff. From it is the saying of the poet:

"When you walk upon the minsa'ah out of old age, Then idle play and flirtation have departed from you."

Likewise, a group of the reciters read without hamza, among them Abu 'Amr and Nafi'. Abu 'Amr said: "I do not know a derivation for it, so I do not hamz it, for if it is of the kind that is hamzated, I have been cautious, since it is not permissible for me to hamz what is not hamzated." Others said: its origin is hamz, and it is from al-minsa'ah with a fatha on the hamza, from "nasa'ta al-ibil wa al-ghanam wa al-naqah" when you drove them. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

"A she-camel firm like the staves of al-Iran, I drove her over a clear path, as if its back were a Burjud (a striped cloak)."

(p-171) It is also transmitted as "wa 'ansin," like "alwah," and its hamza was entirely eased, though analogically it should have been eased intermediately (bayn bayn). The rest of the Seven read it on the original with hamz. Hamza read "minsatahu" with a fatha on the mim and without hamz. A group read "min'saʾatahu" with a silent hamza, and this has no basis except easing by making a moving letter silent without cause, as the poet Imru' al-Qays said:

"Today I drink without being one who bears sin from Allah, nor a loiterer."

A group read "min sa'atihi," with "min" separated and the ta' in "sa'atihi" kasra'd, and this tends toward siyat al-qaws (the notch of the bow), since it is said siyah and sa'ah, so it is as if he said "min sa'atihi," then he made the hamza silent. Its meaning is: from the end of his staff, placing the staff in the position of the bow.

Some people said: Sulayman, peace be upon him, did not die except while travelling, lying down, but he was in a building constructed over him, and the termite ate the threshold of the door until the building collapsed, and thus his death was known. This is weak.

The majority read "tabayyanat al-jinn" with the verb attributed to it, meaning: its matter became clear, as if he said: the jinn were exposed to mankind. This is one interpretation, and it is possible that His saying "tabayyanat al-jinn" means: the jinn knew and became certain, and by "al-jinn" he means their majority, their workers and servants, and by the pronoun in "kanu" he means their leaders and chiefs, because they are the ones who claim knowledge of the unseen for their followers among the jinn and mankind and make them imagine it. This was said by Qatadah, so the followers clearly perceive that the leaders, had they known the unseen, would not have remained (p-172). "An" (that), on the first interpretation, is a substitute for "al-jinn," and on the second interpretation it is a pure object.

Ya'qub read "tubayyinat al-jinn" in the passive voice, meaning: mankind made it clear to them. "An," on this reading, is a substitute, and it may also be in the accusative position with the preposition dropped, i.e., "bi-an," on this reading, and on the first interpretation of the first reading.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The position of Sibawayh is that "an" in this verse has no place in the grammatical structure, and it only signals the answer to what is treated as an oath, from a verb whose meaning is certainty and conviction, because these verbs, namely tabayyantu, tahaqqaqtu, 'alimtu, tayaqqantu and the like, take the place of an oath in your saying: "I knew that if Zayd had stood, 'Amr would not have stood." It is as if you said: "By Allah, if Zayd had stood, 'Amr would not have stood." So His saying "ma labithu" (they would not have remained), on this view, is the answer to what is treated as an oath, not the answer to "law." On the earlier views it is the answer to "law." In the book of al-Nahhas there is an indication that he reads with the accusative "[al-jinn]," i.e., "tabayyanat al-ins al-jinn" (mankind made clear the jinn). "The humiliating punishment" is the labour in that forced servitude. The meaning is that if the jinn knew the unseen, the matter of Sulayman's death would not have been hidden from them, and it has become apparent that it was hidden from them, as they continued in the arduous service while he was dead. Thus "al-muhin" means the one who humiliates, from humiliation (al-hawan). Al-Tabari said: in some readings ["fa-lamma kharra tabayyanat al-ins anna al-jinn law kanu"], and Abu al-Fath reported it from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and Abu Hatim mentioned that it is thus in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. Most exegetes elaborated on the narratives of this verse with things that have no soundness and which the words of the Qur'an do not imply, and there are further meanings after this, so I have abbreviated it for that reason.

[p. 172]

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah Saba', verses 15–17:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿There was indeed a sign for Sheba in their dwelling-place: two gardens, one on the right and one on the left. "Eat from the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him. A good land and a Lord who is Forgiving."﴾ ﴿But they turned away, so We sent upon them the flood of the dam, and We replaced their two gardens with two gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote-trees.﴾ ﴿That is how We repaid them for their disbelief. And do We repay any but the ungrateful?﴾

This is a parable for the Quraysh, with a people whom Allah blessed and to whom He sent messengers, but they disbelieved and turned away, so Allah took vengeance upon them. That is, "You, O people, are like them."

As for "Saba'," here it refers to the tribe. There is a difference of opinion about why the tribe was given this name. One group said it is the name of a woman who was the mother of the tribe. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, in the book of al-Rummani, said it is the name of a place, and the tribe was named after it. The majority said it is the name of a man who was the father of the whole tribe. It was said he was the son of Yashjub ibn Ya'rub. A hadith is also related in support of this view: "The Prophet ﷺ was asked by Furwa ibn Musayk about Saba', what is it? He said: 'It is the name of a man from whom the tribes of Yemen descended.'"

Nafi', 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-A'raj recited "li-Saba'in" with a hamza, nunated and kasra-ended, meaning a living group. Abu 'Amr and al-Hasan recited "li-Saba'" with a hamza, fatha-ended and without nunation, meaning the tribe.

The majority of reciters recited "masakinihim" (their dwelling-places), since each person has a dwelling. al-Kisa'i alone recited "fi maskinihim" with a kasra on the kaf, meaning the place where they lived. This is also the recitation of al-A'mash and 'Alqama. Abu 'Ali said: "The fatha is also good, but this is like how they say 'masjid'" (where a fatha-vowelled form can be used for both the place of prostration and the place itself). Sibawayh, however, considered this to be the name of the house, not the place of prostration. He said: "This is the dialect of people today, and the fatha is the dialect of the Hijaz, which is rare today." Hamza and Hafs recited "maskanahum" with a fatha on the kaf, as a verbal noun. It is a collective noun used to refer to the plural. This is the recitation of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. This singular form is as the poet said:

*"Eat in part of your bellies, that you may be light."*

And as another poet said:

*"The skin of the buffaloes has bitten their necks."*

"Ayah" (sign) means a lesson and a mark of Allah's bounty and power. "Two gardens" is the subject, and its predicate is in His words, "on the right and on the left." Or it is the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: "They are two gardens." This is a sentence meaning: "This is their condition." The substitution (badal) of "ayah" is weak, though Makki and others said it.

﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed clear towns, and We appointed the travel between them: "Travel therein by night and day in security."﴾ ﴿But they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys farther," and they wronged themselves, so We made them into tales and scattered them completely. Surely in that are signs for everyone who is steadfast and thankful.﴾

This verse and what follows describe their condition before the flood (sayl) came. Along with what they were doing, God, blessed and exalted, granted them the two gardens and the blessing particular to them. He had set right the lands connected to them and made them prosperous, made them its masters, and appointed travel within them by bringing the towns close to one another, so that the traveller from Ma'rib to Syria would spend the night in one town and take his midday rest in another, and would not need to carry provisions. "Al-qura" (the towns) means cities, and a small gathering is also called qarya (village), and all of these derive from qaraytu, meaning I gathered. The towns that He blessed are the towns of Syria, by the consensus (ijma') of the exegetes (mufassirun). The "clear towns" (al-qura al-zahira) are those between Syria and Ma'rib, and they are the small ones, which are the open settlements (al-bawadi). Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: they are Arab towns between Medina and Syria, and al-Dahhak said the same. There is disagreement about the meaning of "zahira." One group said: its meaning is elevated, standing high on the hills and knolls, and these are the noblest towns. Another group said: some of them are visible from others, so that they are always within the sight of the traveller, who cannot avoid seeing some part of them in this way. What appears to me is that the meaning of "zahira" is: situated outside the cities. So it refers to the small towns that lie on the outskirts (zawahir) of cities, and the reason the verse distinguishes the small towns by this description from the absolute towns, which are the cities, is that the outskirts of cities are what lies beyond them in the open desert and the plains. From this comes their saying: "We alighted at the outskirts (zahir) of such-and-such a place," meaning outside it. His saying "zahira" is similar to people calling them al-badiya and al-dahiya. From this is the poet's verse:

"Had a band of Quraysh witnessed me, Quraysh of the valley-floors and not Quraysh of the outskirts."

He means those who are outside the valley of Mecca (Batha' Makka). And in the hadith of the rain prayer (istisqa'): "The people of the outskirts (dawahi) came complaining: 'The drowning! The drowning!'"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We appointed the travel therein﴾ means what we have mentioned: that the traveller in it would spend the night in one town and take his midday rest in another, by whatever route he took, without any shortage of this. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Travel therein﴾ means: We said to them. And "[secure]" (amina) means: safe from fear of corrupt people, and secure from hunger, thirst, and the calamities of travel.

Then He related a statement they made in a state of insolence and arrogance, which was asking for greater distance between their journeys, and the report that these distances are far, according to the other readings (qira'at). Nafi', 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ba'id" (make far) with a kasra on the 'ayn, meaning also a request. These two readings mean the same thing: insolence, since they became bored of the blessing of nearness and sought to exchange what is lower for what is better. In the book of al-Rummani it is said that they said: "If the picking of our fruits were farther away, it would be more famous and of greater value." Ibn al-Sumayfa', Sufyan ibn Husayn, Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan (brother of al-Hasan), and Ibn al-Hanafiyya read "Rabbana" in the accusative with "ba'ada" (it became far), with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on the 'ayn, and "bayna" also in the accusative. Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan, from this same group, read "baynu" in the nominative and as an annexed noun to "asfarina." Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Raja', al-Hasan al-Basri, and Ibn al-Hanafiyya also read "Rabbuna" in the nominative with "ba'ada," with a fatha on the 'ayn and the dal. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyya, 'Amr ibn Fa'id, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar also read "Rabbuna" in the nominative with "ba''ada," with a fatha on the 'ayn, a shadda on it, and a fatha on the dal. The meaning of this reading is a report that they considered the near to be far, and saw that this was not satisfying to them, to the extent that it was as if they wanted the towns to be joined to their houses. In this there is excess and resentment toward the decrees (aqdar) and will of God, exalted is He, and little thankfulness for His blessing; rather, it is returning blessing with complaint. In this meaning, and similar to it, along with what was combined with their disbelief, "they wronged themselves," so God, exalted is He, scattered them, ruined their lands, and made them into tales. From this is the well-known proverb: "They were scattered like the hands of Saba'," and "aydi Saba'" is how the proverb is said, in both forms. This is the meaning of their being scattered completely. It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Saba' was the father of ten tribes." When the flood came upon Ma'rib, which is the name of their land, six tribes went to the right (tayammana) of them, meaning they dispersed into the land of Yemen, and four went to the left (tasha'ama) from them. Those who went to the right are Kinda, al-Azd, Ash'ar, Madhhij, and Anmar, from whom came Bajila and Khath'am, and a group called Himyar, which retained the name of the first father. Those who went to the left are Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan, and Khuza'a, who settled in Tihama. From these left-going tribes are the sons of Qayla, namely the Aws and the Khazraj, and from them also 'Amila, and others besides that.

Then God, exalted is He, informed Muhammad (ﷺ), upon whom be prayers and peace, and his community, by way of admonition, that these stories contain signs and lessons for every believer in full. Whoever is characterized by patience and gratitude is the believer who lacks no good quality in any respect.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 34, verses 20–22:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And Iblis certainly found his assumption true concerning them, so they followed him, except a party of the believers﴾ ﴿And he had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it. And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾ ﴿Say: Call upon those you claimed besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have any share in them, nor is there for Him any helper among them﴾

(p-181) Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read: "wa-laqad ṣadaqa" with a light dal, "Iblīsu" in the nominative, and "ẓannahu" in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is also said that it is accusative as an adverb of time or place (ẓarfiyya), meaning: "in his assumption." It is also said that it is accusative as a direct object, in the sense that when he assumed, he acted in a way that confirmed that assumption, as if he only intended that his assumption be true. This is like your saying: "I was wrong in my assumption and I was right in my assumption." 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "ṣaddaqa" with a doubled dal, and "al-ẓann" in this case is the direct object of "ṣaddaqa." This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Talha, ['Asim] and al-A'mash. al-Zuhri, Abu al-Hajhaj and Bilal ibn Abi Burda read: "ṣadaqa" with a light dal, "Iblīsa" in the accusative, and "ẓannuhu" in the nominative. A group read: "ṣadaqa" with a light dal, "Iblīsu" in the nominative, and "ẓannuhu" in the nominative as an apposition, which is a badal al-ishtimal (an apposition of inclusion).

The meaning of the verse is that what Iblis said, that he would mislead the children of Adam and lead them astray, and what he said, that Allah would not find most of them grateful, and other such things, was an assumption on his part, and it proved true concerning them. Allah the Exalted informed us that they followed him, and this was following in disbelief, because the context concerns a disbelieving people. His saying, "from one who is in doubt about it," indicates this. The "min" in His saying "from the believers" is for specifying the kind (bayan al-jins), not for partitioning (tab'id), because partitioning would imply that a party of the believers followed Iblis.

"Sultan" means proof (hujja), and it may also mean dominance and power, since the word derives from "tasallut" (domination). al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he had no whip or sword, but he enticed them, and they inclined to him through his adornment." His saying, "except that We might know," means: that We might know it as existing, since the knowledge of it is prior. A group read: "illā liya'lama" with the ya', in the passive.

His saying, "Say: Call upon those you claimed," is a verse of challenge and establishing proof. It is related that this was revealed at the time of the famine that struck Quraysh. The majority read "qul ud'ū" with a damma on the lam. 'Abbas narrated from Abu 'Amr: "qul ud'ū" with a kasra on the lam. "Those" (alladhīna) refers to the angels and the idols. This is because among Quraysh and the Arabs there were those who worshipped the angels, and among them were those who said: "We worship them so that they may intercede for us," and similar things, so this verse was revealed as a challenge to each of them. Then He described these whom they call gods: that they do not possess ownership of creation, not an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, and that they have no share in them. These two indicate the two types of ownership: either independent ownership or partnership. He negated all of that from them, and He negated that any of them could be a helper to Allah in any part of His power. "Ẓahīr" means helper (mu'in). Then it is further established in the verse that those who assume that they will intercede for them, no intercession from them will be valid for them, since these are disbelievers, and Allah does not permit intercession for a disbeliever.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 34, verse 23:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit, except for him whom He permits; until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say, "What has your Lord said?" They say, "The truth; and He is the Most High, the Most Great."﴾

The meaning: Indeed, all whom you have called upon as gods besides Allah do not possess an atom's weight, and their intercession does not benefit except with permission concerning one who has believed. It is as if He said: "Nor are they intercessors in the sense you supposed."

The interpreters (al-muta'awwilun) differed concerning His words ﴿except for him whom He permits﴾. One group said: its meaning is "for whom He wills." Another group said: its meaning is "for whom He permits to intercede himself."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The wording encompasses both, for when it is taken as relating to the intercessor, there is no doubt that the one interceded for is specified for him; and when it is taken as relating to the one interceded for, the intercessor is necessarily one who knows that specifically. Note that the first lam indicates the one interceded for in His words "li-man" (for whom); you say: "I interceded for so-and-so" (shafa'tu li-fulan).

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "udhina" (أُذِنَ) with a dammah on the alif; Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Ibn 'Amir read "adhina" (أَذِنَ) with a fathah. The pronoun in ﴿"qulubihim"﴾ (their hearts) refers to the angels whom they had called gods. So there is an omission in the speech which the apparent sense indicates; it is as if He said: "Nor are they intercessors as you suppose; rather they are servants and submitters forever, until, when fear is removed from their hearts."

Traditions have been widely reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that this verse, meaning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾, refers only to the angels: when they hear the Revelation, by which Allah commands Gabriel with the matter, they hear something like the dragging of an iron chain over smooth rock, and they are then seized with fear out of reverence and awe. It was said: out of fear that the Hour may have come. When that is over, fear is removed from their hearts, i.e., the fear is lifted from them and uncovered; so some of them say to others, and to Gabriel: ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾ The ones questioned reply: "He has said the truth, ﴿and He is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾" With this meaning, of mentioning the angels at the beginning of the verses, this verse coheres with the first explanation. Whoever does not perceive that the angels are indicated from the beginning of His words ﴿"those you claimed"﴾ [Saba': 22] will not find this verse connected to what precedes it, and that is why the exegetes were confused in explaining it, to the point that some said, concerning the disbelievers, after the arrival of death: "fear is removed from their hearts through the loss of life, so they see the reality, and their fear of the doubts that were raised for them during their lives departs; so they will be told then: ﴿'What has your Lord said?'﴾ and they will say: 'He has said the truth,' acknowledging it when acknowledgment no longer benefits them." Another group said: the verse concerns all of creation, and His words ﴿"until, when"﴾ mean: on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first interpretation, concerning the angels, is the correct one, and it is the one to which the traditions are widely attested. These two are remote.

The majority read ﴿"fuzzi'a"﴾ with a dammah on the fa' and a kasrah on the zay, meaning: fear has been removed from them. These verbs came in contrast to other verbs, because "fa''ala" originally means causing entry into a thing, whereas your saying "fazza'tu Zaydan" means: I removed fear from him. Allah the Exalted says:

﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah. And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in manifest error.﴾ ﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we committed in sin, nor will we be questioned about what you do.﴾ ﴿Say: Our Lord will bring us together, then He will judge between us in truth, and He is the All-Knowing Judge.﴾ ﴿Say: Show me those whom you have joined to Him as partners. No! Rather, He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

Allah, blessed and exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ), by way of argumentation and establishing proof, concerning the One who provides for them from the heavens and the earth, [that he should ask them]: "Who is He?" Then He commanded him to cut short the argument by giving the answer to the question, since they are in a state of bewilderment and confusion regarding the question, and they have no answer, nor does anyone of sound nature, except by saying: "He is Allah." This is the method for every question whose answer is extremely clear, because the one presenting the argument wants to cut it short and move on to another proof that he will present. Similar examples of this in the Qur'an are numerous.

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, we or you﴾, it is a gentle approach in the call and in the discourse, and the meaning is like when you say to someone who disagrees with you on a matter: "One of us is mistaken," meaning: be careful and pay attention, while what is understood from your speech is that your opponent is the one in error. Thus this means: "Indeed we are upon guidance or in manifest error, and indeed you are upon guidance or in manifest error, so let us examine it." The intent is that the error lies within the sphere of those addressed, and one of the two predicates was omitted because the remaining one indicates it. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Aw" (or) in the verse has the meaning of the conjunctive "wa" (and), and the estimated sense is: "Indeed we and you are upon guidance or in manifest error," and these are two predicates that are not of two subjects. This view is not convincing, and the wording does not support it, although the meaning, according to every view, requires that guidance lies within the sphere of the believers and error within the sphere of the disbelievers.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we committed in sin﴾ and the rest of the verse, it is a truce and a disengagement, and it has been abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) by the verse of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*).

As for His saying: ﴿Say: Our Lord will bring us together﴾ and the rest of the verse, it is a report about the resurrection from the graves. His saying "yaftah" (He will judge) means He will decide, and al-Fattah means the judge, and this usage is well known in the dialect of Yemen. All of this has been abrogated by the sword.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: Show me﴾, it may be a sight of the heart, in which case His saying "shuraka'" (partners) is the third object (*maf'ul thalith*), and this is the correct view; that is, "Show me with proof and evidence how the partnership is." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 34, verses 28–30:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, but most of mankind do not know﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "For you is the appointment of a Day from which you cannot delay by an hour or advance."﴾

This is an announcement from Allah, blessed and exalted, that He sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to all the world. "Al-kaffah" (the comprehensive, all-inclusive) means the most complete form of humankind. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), and He placed it first for emphasis. This is one of the distinctive qualities with which Muhammad (ﷺ) was singled out among the prophets, which he (ﷺ) summed up in his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I have been given five things that no one before me was given: I was made victorious through terror (ar-ru'b) over a distance of a month's journey; spoils of war were made lawful for me, though they were not lawful for anyone before me; I was given jawami' al-kalim (comprehensive speech in few words); the earth was made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification; and every prophet was sent only to a particular people, while I was sent to the red and the black." In Muslim's collection there is an addition to these qualities.

His words, ﴿but most of mankind do not know﴾, are meant in a general sense regarding the disbelievers, while the believers are the minority.

Then He related their statement, mocking the matter of the Resurrection and hastening it, in the sense of denial, with their words: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ So Allah, exalted, commanded His Prophet to inform them of the appointment of a Day, which is the Day of Resurrection, from which no one can delay or advance.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "al-wa'd" (promise), "al-wa'id" (threat) and "al-mi'ad" (appointment) have the same meaning. This has been disputed. What the people hold is that al-wa'd is used for good, al-wa'id for what is disliked, and al-mi'ad applies to both. He attributed the appointment to the day by metonymy (tajawwuz), since it occurs within it. The verse may also be understood as the disbelievers hastening the punishment of this world, and the answer would then also concern that. On this interpretation, however, no mention of the Resurrection would have been made.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 34, verses 31–32:

His Mighty and Majestic saying:

﴿And those who disbelieved said, "We will never believe in this Qur'an or in that which came before it." If you could but see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, returning word to one another. Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Were it not for you, we would have been believers."﴾ ﴿Those who were arrogant will say to those who were oppressed, "Did we avert you from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you were criminals."﴾

In this verse is related a statement made by some of the Quraysh, namely that they do not believe in the Qur'an nor in what is before it of the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. It is as if they denied all the Books of Allah. They did this when the argument against them was made by what is in the Torah concerning the matter of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace.

A group said: "That which is before it (alladhi bayna yadayhi)" refers to the Hour and the Resurrection. This is an error, for the one who said it did not understand the meaning of "before the hand (bayna al-yad)" in the language, that it means what precedes in time. We have already explained its meaning in what came before.

Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, informed His Prophet about the state of the wrongdoers, in the form of expressing wonder at their condition. The response to "law" (lau, "if") is omitted. The phrase ﴿returning word to one another﴾ means they are conversing and disputing with one another. Then He explained that dispute: the followers and the weak among the disbelievers say to the disbelievers and to the leaders, by way of blame, reproach and turning the reproach back upon them: "Were it not for you, we would have believed and been guided." That is: you misled us and commanded us to disbelieve. The leaders then say to them, by way of rebuke and denial: "Did we avert you from guidance?" Rather, you were criminals; that is, you entered into disbelief with your own insight, and you committed crime by your own consideration. Our invitation was not a compulsion (darbat lazib) upon you, because we called you without any proof or evidence. All of this is contained in the wording.

(p-191) The words of the Most High:

﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them, those will be brought to the punishment.﴾ ﴿Say: Indeed my Lord extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants, and restricts it for him. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers.﴾

When the Most High mentioned the believers who do righteous deeds and their reward, He followed it by mentioning their opposites and their recompense, so that the difference in ranks would become clear. A group read "mu'ājizīn" (مُعاجِزِينَ), and another group read "mu'jizīn" (مُعَجِّزِينَ), and their explanation has already been given.

And "muḥḍarūn" (مُحْضَرُونَ) is from ihḍār (الإحْضار), meaning bringing forth and preparing.

Then He repeated the statement about the extension and restriction of provision, for emphasis and clarification, and here He intends by it the provision of the believers. Its context is not the first meaning, which was brought for the disbelievers. Rather, this here is by way of admonition and encouraging detachment from the world, and urging spending in acts of obedience. Then He promised a replacement for that, and it is on the condition of moderation (al-iqtiṣād), intention in obedience, and warding off harms; it is a promise that will certainly be fulfilled, either in this world or in the Hereafter. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah said to me: Spend, and I will spend upon you," and in al-Bukhārī: "Indeed an angel calls out every day: O Allah, give the one who spends a replacement; and another angel says: O Allah, give the one who withholds destruction."

As for His saying: ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾, it is because it is said of a person that he provides for his dependents, and a commander provides for his soldiers; but that is from property over which he has been given ownership, whereas Allah, the Most High, provides from treasuries that do not perish, and by bringing things out from non-existence into existence. Al-A'mash read "wa-yuqaddiru" (وَيُقَدِّرُ) with a damma on the yā' and a shaddah on the dāl.

(p-192) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And on the Day He will gather them all together, then He will say to the angels, "Did these worship you?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."﴾ ﴿So today none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another. And We will say to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs, they say, "This is none but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship." And they say, "This is nothing but a fabricated lie." And those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾

This is a verse of warning to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: "Mention the day..." The majority (al-Jumhur) read "naḥshuruhum" and "thumma naqūlu" with the nun in both, and Abu Bakr narrated it from 'Asim. Ḥafs read it from 'Asim with the ya' in both, and Abu Ḥatim mentioned it from Abu 'Amr.

The saying to the angels is a question by which the proof is established against the disbelievers, their worshippers, similar to His Exalted saying to 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116]. When Allah Exalted says this statement to the angels, the angels say: ﴿"Glory be to You,"﴾ meaning: an exoneration of You from what these disbelievers did. Then they cleared themselves by their saying: ﴿"You are our Guardian, not them."﴾ They intend disassociation from having any knowledge, consent, or participation in being worshipped by mankind. Then they established that mankind worshipped the jinn only by the consent of the jinn and by their seducing mankind. So the angels did not deny that mankind worshipped them; rather, they established that they had no participation in that. Then they made the jinn responsible. The worship of mankind toward the jinn, as we understand it, is by obeying them, listening to their whisperings and seductions; this is a type of worship. It is possible that among the disbelieving nations there were those who worshipped the jinn, and there are verses in the Qur'an that show this, in al-An'am and elsewhere.

Then He, glorified be He, said: "So today," and there is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied meaning being: "then it will be said to them," that is, to those who worshipped and those who were worshipped: ﴿none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another.﴾

His Exalted saying: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾. In this verse He mentions their sayings and kinds of speech when the Qur'an is recited to them and they hear its wisdom and its clear proofs. One of them slandered the Prophet ﷺ, saying that he disparages the idols and the religion of the fathers; another slandered him by saying that this Qur'an is fabricated, i.e., made up by Muhammad, and he claims it is from God; and another slandered him by saying that what he has of softness, attracting souls and winning over hearing, is only magic, by which he draws and summons. Exalted is Allah above their sayings, and His Law is sanctified above their slander.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 34, verses 44–46**

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿We did not give them books that they study, nor did We send to them any warner before you.﴾ ﴿Those before them denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them, yet they denied My messengers. So how was My rejection?﴾ ﴿Say: I admonish you with only one thing: that you stand before God in pairs and singly, then reflect: there is no madness in your companion. He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment.﴾

The meaning of this verse is that they speak about the Book of God, may He be blessed and exalted, according to their own opinions. Some of them say it is magic and others say it is fabrication. This is audacity on their part, for they do not rest on any trace of knowledge nor on the report of anyone whose report is accepted. We did not give them books that they study, nor did We send to them a warner, so that they could claim that their statements rest on his command.

The majority of readers recited ﴿يَدْرُسُونَها﴾ (yadrusunaha, "they study it") with a sukun on the dal. Abu Haywa recited ﴿يُدَّرِسُونَها﴾ (yuddarisunaha) with a fatha on the dal, a shadda, and a kasra on the ra'. The meaning is: We did not send a warner who addresses them directly with anything, or who associates with the people of their time or with those near to their forefathers. Otherwise, warning has existed in the world and among the Arabs, with Shu'ayb, Salih and Hud, and the call to God and His oneness is an ancient matter; the earth has never been without someone calling to it. So the meaning is: a warner who is specific to those to whom We have sent you. Among the Arabs there was much of the warning of Isma'il, peace be upon him, and God, the Exalted, says: ﴿He was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 54]. However, none devoted himself entirely to warning, nor fought for it, except Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him.

Then He gave them the example of the nations that denied before them. His words ﴿وَما بَلَغُوا مِعْشارَ ما آتَيْناهُمْ﴾ ("they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them") allow three meanings. The first is that the pronoun in ﴿بَلَغُوا﴾ ("they reached") refers to the Quraysh, and the pronoun in ﴿آتَيْناهُمْ﴾ ("We had given them") refers to the nations before them. The meaning is: in terms of strength, blessings and prominence in this world. This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, may God be pleased with them. The second is the reverse: the meaning is in terms of the signs, clear proofs and light that you brought them. The third is that the pronoun refers to the earlier nations, and the meaning is: in terms of the gratitude for the blessing and the return for the favour. The word ﴿المِعْشارُ﴾ (al-mi'shar, "the tenth") means one tenth. This pattern (mif'al) occurs only with the numbers ten and four, so they said mirba' (a quarter) and mi'shar (a tenth). Some people said that al-mi'shar is a tenth of a tenth, but this is nothing.

The word ﴿النَكِيرُ﴾ (al-nakir, "the rejection") is a verbal noun with the meaning of al-inkar (denial), and it has the pattern of ʿarin. The yā' was dropped from it for lightness, because it is the end of a verse. The word ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ (kayfa, "how") here expresses magnification of the matter, and it is not a plain interrogative. In this there is a threat to the Quraysh, meaning: they are exposed to a rejection like it.

Then He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to call them to the worship of God and to reflect on the reality of his own prophethood, and to admonish them with a matter that is close to understanding. So His words ﴿بِواحِدَةٍ﴾ ("with one thing") mean: with one single matter, in brevity for you and in facilitation for you. His words ﴿أنْ﴾ ("that") are explanatory (mufassira), and it is permissible that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿واحِدَةٍ﴾. His words ﴿تَقُومُوا لِلَّهِ مَثْنى وفُرادى﴾ ("you stand before God in pairs and singly") may mean standing in obedience, sincerity and worship. In that case, the one thing with which he admonishes is this, and then he joins to it that they reflect on his own affair: is there madness in him, or is he free of that? The pause in the view of Abu Hatim is at ﴿تَتَفَكَّرُوا﴾ ("then reflect"), so ﴿ما بِصاحِبِكُمْ﴾ ("there is no madness in your companion") becomes a new negation. According to Sibawayh, it is the answer to what has taken the place of an oath, because ﴿تَفَكَّرَ﴾ (tafakkara, "reflected") is among the verbs that give certainty, like ﴿تَبَيَّنَ﴾ (tabayyana, "became clear"). On this view, the reflection is on the signs of God and belief in Him. It is also possible that by their standing for the sake of God's face he means the reflection on Muhammad, peace be upon him. In that case, the one thing with which he admonished is "that they stand," meaning: that you stand for the purpose of reflection on the matter of your need. It is as if the meaning is that each one reflects between himself and his own soul, and two people debate each other seeking verification: is there madness in Muhammad, ﷺ, or not? On this view, one does not stop at ﴿تَفَكَّرُوا﴾.

He mentioned the dual first, because the truths are more fruitful when two who support each other examine them than a single thought. When the truth becomes clear between the two, each of them then reflects afterwards, and so his insight increases. The poet said:

When they gather, they bring every strange thing,
so some of the people increase in knowledge from others.

Ya'qub recited ﴿ثُمَّ تَفَكَّرُوا﴾ with a single ta'. Mujahid said that ﴿بِواحِدَةٍ﴾ means: "there is no god but God." It was said other than this, which the verse does not indicate.

His words ﴿بَيْنَ يَدَيْ﴾ ("before") are connected to the fact that Muhammad ﷺ came in time before the severe punishment with which they were threatened.

The Exalted said:

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 34, verse 52–54:

(p-197) His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And they will say, "We believe in Him." But how can they reach [Him] from a distant place?﴾ ﴿And they had already disbelieved in Him before, and they used to hurl [assumptions] about the unseen from a distant place.﴾ ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their counterparts before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.﴾

The pronoun in "bihi" (in Him) refers to Allah, the Exalted, in the phrase "bihi." It was also said that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), his law (shar'), and the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, and the majority of reciters read "at-tanaush" with a damma on the waw and without a hamza. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and also 'Asim (in another transmission) read it with a hamza. The first reading means "at-tanaawul" (reaching, taking hold), from their saying: "nasha yanushu" when one reaches for something, and "tanawasha al-qawm fi al-harb" when the people in battle lay hold of one another with weapons. From this is the poet's verse:

"She reaches for the pool, reaching from on high, a reach by which she cuts across the wide deserts."

So it is as if he said: "How can they attain their desire, while they have moved far from the place where such attainment is possible?" As for the reading with a hamza, it may be from the same root, with the waw made into a hamza because it bears a permanent damma, as they said: "uqqatat" and other similar forms. It may also be from seeking (at-talab); one says "tana'asht al-shay'" when one seeks a thing from afar. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "tana'ush al-shay'" is its returning, related from him by Ibn al-Anbari, who recited:

"She wishes that Mayy would return to you, but there is no way to reach her return."

So it is as if he said in the verse: "How can they seek their desire, when it has become distant?" Mujahid said: the meaning is: from the Hereafter to this world.

The majority read "wa yaqdhifuna" with a fatha on the ya and a kasra on the dhal, attributing the verb to them, meaning: they hurl [accusations] by their assumptions, and they cast these at the Messenger and the Book of Allah, while that is unseen to them, in their saying: "sorcery," "fabrication," and other such things. This was said by Mujahid. Qatada said: their casting about the unseen is their saying: "There is no resurrection, no Paradise, and no Fire." Mujahid read it with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the dhal, meaning: the revelation will pelt them with what they dislike from the heaven.

As for His saying: "And a barrier will be placed between them..." (the verse). Al-Hasan said: its meaning is: [a barrier between them and] faith, repentance, returning to trustworthiness, and righteous deeds, because they desired it at a time when repentance does not benefit. Qatada also said this. Mujahid said: its meaning is: a barrier between them and the bounties and pleasures of this world. It was also said: a barrier between them and Paradise and its bounties. This is very fitting according to the view that the seizing and terror mentioned refers to the Day of Resurrection.

As for His saying: "as was done with their counterparts," i.e., the groups resembling them from every nation, and it is the plural of "shi'a" (party).
